Practice passages (invented for this exercise; the numbers are NOT from real studies). Should students be allowed to use a calculator on every math test?

Passage A. In a school trial, students who used calculators finished a 20-question test in 35 minutes instead of 50, and made 3 times fewer arithmetic slips. Most jobs that use maths also use a calculator or a spreadsheet.

Passage B. In the same school, 30% of the students who used calculators on every test could not do a simple multiplication by hand at the end of the term. Teachers said these students had stopped checking whether an answer made sense.

content.question: Which is the strongest REPLY to that counter-argument?
choices: B) However, students can keep their skills by estimating first, because an estimate shows whether the calculator answer makes sense.

content.content: Words to symbols. “A less than B” means B − A (the order flips). “Twice n” = 2n. “The sum of n and 4, times 6” = 6(n + 4). Distribute: 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6. pomodoros.subject: Science: atoms and chemical change; speed

content.content: Everything is made of atoms. An atom has protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge) in its centre, and electrons (negative charge) moving around it. The number of protons is the atomic number, and it decides which element the atom is: 6 protons is carbon, 8 protons is oxygen. The mass number is protons plus neutrons. In a physical change (ice melting, paper tearing) no new substance forms. In a chemical change (iron rusting, wood burning) a new substance forms, often with a colour change, gas or heat. Speed = distance ÷ time. On the pH scale, below 7 is acid, 7 is neutral and above 7 is a base.

pomodoros.subject: Reading and Vocabulary: Marie Maynard Daly

content.content: Marie Maynard Daly was born on April 16, 1921, in Queens, New York. Her father, Ivan Daly, loved science. He had won a scholarship to study chemistry at Cornell University, but he could not afford to finish. Marie went on to Columbia University, and in 1947 she became the first Black woman in the United States to earn a PhD in chemistry. She went on to study how the body works at the chemical level, including cholesterol and heart disease, and she researched high blood pressure. In 1988 she set up a scholarship at Queens College in the name of her parents, Ivan C. and Helen H. Daly, to support students in the physical sciences. She died in 2003. (Practice passage written for this packet from published sources: Science History Institute, 2024; Science News, 2022.)
